3.3 TENSTALLATION OF DRAIN LINERS
3.3.1 Summary

During tne installation of the trial norizontal drains, proplems
arose whicn were not anticipated, and some predicted problems did not
occur. At the peginning of tne trial, the main concern was the provision
of a horizontal drain which would not clog and would prevent the loss of
fines througn its openings. nis did not prove to pve a proplen in the
short term, out PVC drain liners were found to be of inadequate strength.
In order to install 70 m drains under the conditions prevailing at the
site, it was found necessary to use drain liners made of a stronger
material.

The original requirement of providing a drain with openings only
along the top lost priority, as screens were eventually placed totally
pelow the water table, the major part of the drain liner being
unperforated. An adequate drain detail was finally achieved after much
experimentation.

Originally, tne type of drain considered as ideal nad a perforated
upper portion and an impervious invert, which ensured that all draining
water flowed in the drain and could not infiltrate into the soil closer to
tne slope surface. As a horizontal drain liner is necessarily smaller
than the nole in wnich it is placed, an annular void will exist between
tne external wall of the drain liner and the formed hole. If the lower
nalf of this annulus is left ungrouted and tne soil surrounding tne hole
does not collapse onto the drain liner, water intercepted by the drainage
nole will pe conducted along this void regardless of wnetner or not the
invert of the drain liner is solid and will infiltrate into the slope
nearer the slope surface. However, the American literature, wnicn is tne
most comprehensive on horizontal drain installations, does not mention the
use of grouted laperimeaple drain inverts. One can only assume that tnese
nave never been used or considered in the USA, although perforations are
confined to the tops of the pipes. In fact, the only papers demonstrating
the need for, and detailing the construction of, such an invert were found
in Hong Kong publications (Choi, 1974; Tong & Maher, 1975). Herbert
(1982) of the Institute of Geological Sciences, England, confirmed that
the efficiency of norizontal drains in dewatering that part of the slope
below the drain is dependant on making the drain invert impermeaple.
However, he questioned the practicality of doing this and suggested that
it would be easier to make the drain liner unperforated above the water
table and then fully grout this portion.
